summary: Defines NETCONF Call Home and RESTCONF Call Home, which let a server open the secure connection to the client instead of the client connecting first. This helps with devices behind firewalls.

eli5.summary: Instead of you calling a device, the device calls you, which helps when it hides behind a locked door.

questions: what ports does netconf call home use
how does restconf call home work
subtitle: Lets a managed device dial out to its NETCONF or RESTCONF manager, which helps behind firewalls and NAT.

tldr.problem: Network devices behind firewalls or NAT, or with changing addresses, cannot easily be reached by a management system that has to connect to them first.
tldr.mechanism: The NETCONF or RESTCONF server opens the TCP connection to the client. After that, the client starts SSH or TLS and then NETCONF or RESTCONF, so every other role stays unchanged.
tldr.outcome: The RFC assigns three TCP ports, 4334, 4335 and 4336, and requires the client to validate the server's host key or certificate.

today: RFC 8071 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reversing Who Connects First
sections.content:
NETCONF Call Home and RESTCONF Call Home let a NETCONF or RESTCONF server initiate a secure connection to a client. NETCONF Call Home works over both of NETCONF's secure transports, SSH and TLS. RESTCONF Call Home supports only TLS, like RESTCONF itself.

Only one role is reversed: at the TCP layer, the server is the TCP client. The device is still the SSH or TLS server and still the NETCONF or RESTCONF server. Because those roles do not change, existing certificate chains and user authentication mechanisms are unaffected.

The RFC says this applies only to NETCONF and RESTCONF. Base SSH and TLS do not require programmatic verification of the other party, so letting an SSH or TLS server contact the client for other purposes needs a thorough contextual risk assessment. The text also notes that the statement in RFC 4253 that the client initiates the connection does not apply here.
sections.eli5: Only the first phone call is flipped. After that, who is the server and who is the client works exactly as before.

sections.title: Why Devices Call Home
sections.content:
The RFC lists scenarios that call home enables:

  • A new device registers itself with its management system after first power-on.
  • A device gets an IP address dynamically and does not register it in a mapping service such as dynamic DNS.
  • A device sits behind a firewall that does NAT, or behind one that allows no management access inward.
  • A device runs in stealth mode with no open ports.
  • An operator prefers to secure one open port in the data center rather than one on every device.
sections.eli5: Some devices hide behind locked doors or move around. It is easier for them to call out than for the boss to find them.

sections.title: The Call Home Sequence
sections.content:
Call home runs in three steps. First, the server initiates a TCP connection to the client. Second, over that connection, the client initiates an SSH or TLS session to the server. Third, over that session, the client initiates a NETCONF or RESTCONF session to the server.

At the SSH/TLS and NETCONF/RESTCONF layers, arrows still point from client to server, as in a normal connection. The RFC uses "NETCONF/RESTCONF" as shorthand and does not require an implementation to support both protocols.
sections.eli5: The device dials first. Then the manager picks up and starts the secure conversation, then the real management chat begins.

sections.title: What Client and Server Must Do
sections.content:
The client listens for TCP connections from servers. It MUST support accepting connections on the IANA-assigned ports but MAY listen elsewhere. When it accepts one, it starts the SSH client or TLS client protocol. With TLS, the client MUST advertise peer_allowed_to_send from RFC 6520, so servers can rely on keep-alives, which are needed most in call home.

The client MUST validate the server's host key or certificate, either by certificate path validation or by comparing against a previously trusted ("pinned") value. If a certificate has been revoked, the client MUST close the connection immediately. With path validation, the certificate must chain to a preconfigured issuer and encode an identifier the client knew before the attempt. Client credentials MUST only be ones previously associated with that host key or certificate.

The server starts the connection from a source port set by local policy or chosen randomly. It MUST support connecting to the IANA-assigned ports. It sends its host key or certificate, and, for a certificate, all intermediate certificates up to a well-known trusted issuer. If transport-level client authentication is required and fails within a time set by local policy, the server MUST close the connection.

For a persistent connection, the server SHOULD test liveness. On TLS it SHOULD send HeartbeatRequest messages. On SSH it SHOULD send an SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST with a deliberately nonexistent request name and the want-reply value set to 1.
sections.eli5: The manager listens for calls and checks the device's ID carefully before trusting it. The device keeps poking the line now and then to make sure the call is still alive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Having the SSH/TLS server open the TCP connection departs from RFC 4253 and from RFC 6125, where the client builds its reference identifiers independently of what the service presents. The risk centers on server authentication. The mitigation is the mandatory host key or certificate validation, and, with certificates, matching an identifier such as a serial number that the client was preconfigured to expect.

Clients should make sure the preconfigured issuer certificate is unique to the server's manufacturer, not a third-party authority that issues for several manufacturers. Otherwise a client using a password-style login could send its shared secret to another server with the same identity.

Internet-facing hosts will be fingerprinted by scanning tools. SSH and TLS clients may be less robust than servers, so update mechanisms matter. An attacker could try to make the client do expensive operations, a denial-of-service risk, and the RFC recommends precautions such as temporarily blocking a source address after repeated failed logins. With RESTCONF, special care is needed with HTTP schemes that convey a shared secret, such as Basic and Digest.
sections.eli5: Since the device calls the manager, the manager must make sure the caller is really the right device. It should also be careful about handing out passwords and about people who call just to waste its time.

sections.title: The Three Assigned Ports
sections.content: IANA assigned three TCP port numbers in the User Ports range, which become the default ports for call home: netconf-ch-ssh on 4334, netconf-ch-tls on 4335 and restconf-ch-tls on 4336. The port also tells both sides which protocols to start: 4334 means SSH then NETCONF, 4335 means TLS then NETCONF, and 4336 means TLS then RESTCONF.
sections.eli5: Each of three phone extensions means a different kind of call, so both sides know what kind of conversation to start.
